clue.text: The very worst surprise — refraining from booze has brought about success; …

parts.note: to rock someone is to shock or surprise them

indicators.note: the success word is brought around the abstinence letters, enclosing them

parts.note: a boom is a time of great success or prosperity
TT, teetotal, describes someone who abstains from alcohol

explanation.surface: A shock: someone giving up drink has turned out to be a triumph, and the sentence runs on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has brought about' is containment here. TT for teetotal is a crossword staple; the ellipsis only carries the surface into 6 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: reaching the lowest possible point or level is hitting rock bottom, the very worst state.

clue.text: Work in series picking up strands

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
in a down clue, picking up means the letters are lifted and read upwards

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A worker on a production line picks up loose threads one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picking up' reads upwards in a down light, giving RES; 'in' then houses the work abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: thick twisted cords, made of several strands, are ropes, and a strand of rope can stand for the whole.

clue.text: Singer is tense during difficult work, ending in despair

indicators.note: the letters for is and tense come during, that is inside, the word for difficult work

parts.note: a chore is a tedious or difficult task
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: only the final letter of despair is used

explanation.surface: A singer gets tense in the middle of a tough job and ends up despairing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' signals the insertion, and 'ending in' supplies R from despair.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a chorister is a singer in a choir, especially a church choir.

clue.text: Patrol yonder to handle call to move forces

parts.note: a beat is a police officer's patrol route
yonder means over there
to treat someone is to handle or deal with them

explanation.surface: A patrol over there is told to respond to an order to redeploy troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Military term: beating the retreat was a drum signal ordering troops back to camp, now a ceremonial parade.

clue.text: Time attention given to gossip — it'll make you weep

parts.note: giving someone an ear means listening to them attentively
gas is idle chatter or gossip

explanation.surface: Listening to tittle-tattle for too long is enough to reduce anyone to tears.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a chemical irritant used in riot control stings the eyes and causes tears.

clue.text: Like dental treatment? Sadly I do not, beginning to cry

indicators.note: taken as an adverb of something going wrong, it tells us to rearrange the letters
only the first letter of cry is taken

explanation.surface: A nervous patient admits sadly that they do not like the dentist, and starts to cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' rearranges I DO NOT into ODONTI, and 'beginning to' adds C from cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective sense: odontic means relating to teeth, so dental work is of that kind.

clue.text: … success not entirely unexpected? Excellent

parts.note: making a go of something is making a success of it

indicators.note: the word for unexpected is not given in full, losing its final letter

parts.note: something odd is strange or unexpected

explanation.surface: Continuing from 1 across: the triumph was hardly a surprise, and that is excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' trims ODD to OD.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something excellent is very good, of high quality.

clue.text: Nothing published? That'll restrict good newspaper, perhaps

parts.note: O, the figure zero, stands for nothing

indicators.note: the word for published is said to hold in, or restrict, the letter for good

parts.note: a paper that ran a story published it

explanation.surface: An editor worries that printing nothing will hamper a decent newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That'll restrict' puts G inside RAN, giving RGAN after O.
explanation.definitionFit: Sense: an organ is a periodical that speaks for a group, and a newspaper is one example.

clue.text: Neglect trendy guy concealing last of horrible fat

indicators.note: the guy's letters wrap around and hide the other pieces

parts.note: a dude is a fashion-conscious man

indicators.note: only the final letter of horrible is used

parts.note: suet is hard animal fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: A fashionable man hides some disgusting fat and ignores it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing' signals the insertion; 'last of' supplies E from horrible.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: desuetude is a state of disuse or neglect, as with a law no longer enforced.

clue.text: Ways to handle blows long protecting daughter — manages to avoid first

indicators.note: the word for long wraps around the daughter letter as if shielding it

parts.note: to long for something is to hanker after it

indicators.note: the word for manages loses its opening letter

parts.note: someone who manages a task achieves it

explanation.surface: A parent weathering lengthy punches while shielding their daughter somehow dodges the first one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blows' looks like punches, but these are nose-blows. 'protecting' puts D in HANKER; 'to avoid first' cuts ACHIEVES to CHIEVES.
explanation.definitionFit: Pun: a hanky is what you use when you blow your nose, so these are means of dealing with blows.

clue.text: Stupid article about soldiers is taken in proportion

indicators.note: the fool and the article go around the soldiers' letters

parts.note: a prat is a stupid person, British slang
OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A daft newspaper piece about the army gets things in proportion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the insertion. The noun for a fool is British slang, standing in for the adjective 'Stupid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin phrase: pro rata means proportionally, shared out according to each part's size.

clue.text: Fruit — old types available?

parts.note: a shop's ranges are the types of product it has available

explanation.surface: A shopper asks whether any heritage varieties of fruit are in stock.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: oranges are citrus fruit.

clue.text: Family time in view, though not hanging loose

indicators.note: the family and time letters go in the word for view

parts.note: a sight is a view or spectacle
kin are one's family or relatives

explanation.surface: Relatives come into view, though their clothes don't hang loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the insertion; 'though' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: clothing that is skintight clings closely to the body rather than hanging loose.

clue.text: One failing to study introduction of culture in classic SF novel

indicators.note: that letter goes inside the novel's title

parts.note: Dune is Frank Herbert's science fiction novel

indicators.note: only the opening letter of culture is used

explanation.surface: A student flounders over an introduction to the culture in a famous science fiction book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts C, from 'introduction of culture', inside DUNE.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a dunce is a slow learner, someone who fails at their studies.

clue.text: Have some aspiration, but not about to take to the sea?

indicators.note: the letters for about are not included

parts.note: aspiration is breathing, so to have some is to breathe
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone with an ambition to swim hesitates over going into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aspiration' looks like ambition but here means breathing. 'not' removes RE from BREATHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sense: to bathe, in British use, is to swim in the sea, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Jerk getting his leg broken in winter sports vehicle

parts.note: to bob is to make a quick jerking movement

indicators.note: the letters of his leg are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: An idiot breaks his leg in a winter sports sled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an idiot but is a verb, BOB. 'broken' rearranges HIS LEG.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a bobsleigh is a steerable sled raced down an ice track in winter sports.

clue.text: Curse able to be translated — thus?

definitions.text: Curse able to be translated — thus?

indicators.note: translating turns the words into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A curse that can be put into another language: and here is how it looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be translated' rearranges CURSE ABLE; the result is a French oath, so the clue is its own definition.
explanation.definitionFit: French exclamation: this mild oath of surprise or annoyance is literally a curse rendered in French.

clue.text: Caledonia possibly neither cold nor hot?

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Scotland's weather may be judged lukewarm at best.
explanation.walkthrough: Caledonia is the Latin name for Scotland. 'possibly' rearranges its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Biblical allusion: the church at Laodicea was rebuked as lukewarm, so the word means half-hearted, indifferent.

clue.text: Ludicrous problem handed back by the French — entirely not getting it

indicators.note: the word for problem is returned, read backwards

parts.note: a rub is a snag or difficulty, as in Hamlet's 'there's the rub'
les is French for 'the' (plural)

indicators.note: the word for entirely leaves out the letters of it

parts.note: quite means entirely or completely

explanation.surface: A daft problem is passed back by the French, who quite fail to understand it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handed back' turns RUB into BUR; 'not getting' removes IT from QUITE, leaving QUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective sense: burlesque means mocking through absurd exaggeration, so comically ludicrous.

clue.text: Former hunt runs out over weir

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first part sits over the second
the letter for runs is taken out of the hunt's name

parts.note: the Quorn is a famous English foxhunt in Leicestershire
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a dam, like a weir, holds back a river

explanation.surface: An old hunt flees across a weir.
explanation.walkthrough: The Quorn is a well-known English foxhunt. 'out' removes R, leaving QUON, and 'over' places it above DAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: quondam is a literary word meaning former or one-time.

clue.text: Police in favour of blocking criminal without using fine

definitions.note: used as a verb, to control or keep in order

indicators.note: the letters for in favour of sit within the criminal word, blocking it
the criminal word is used without the letter for fine

parts.note: a fence is a criminal who receives stolen goods
F is an abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
for means in favour of

explanation.surface: Police who support blocking a criminal manage without imposing a fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without using' leaves ENCE, and 'blocking' signals the insertion. A fence is a receiver of stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb synonym: to police a rule is to make sure it is obeyed.

clue.text: Unmatched, as applied to carbon copy

indicators.note: the single word is attached to the carbon letter

parts.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon
lone means single, without a partner

explanation.surface: A singular item is said to be the same as a carbon copy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carbon copy' reads as one phrase, but carbon supplies C and copy alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a clone is an exact replica or copy.

clue.text: Edible seaweed making you salivate? Not at first

indicators.note: the word for salivate is used without its opening letter

parts.note: to slaver is to drool or salivate

explanation.surface: A seaweed so tasty it makes your mouth water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not at first' removes S from SLAVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: laver is a red seaweed eaten in Wales as laverbread.

clue.text: Very brash response regarding some sweater design

parts.note: neck, as in brass neck, is cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: A cheeky retort about a knitting pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass neck is British slang for brazen cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a neckline cut in a V shape is a common design for jumpers.

clue.text: Not working with German in league is not to be considered

parts.note: a machine that is off is not working

indicators.note: the German word goes inside the other letters

parts.note: mit is German for with

explanation.surface: An idle German club member is ruled out of consideration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with German' asks for the German word, not an abbreviation for German; 'in' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a topic that is off limits is forbidden, not open for discussion.

clue.text: Obstruct display of goods

definitions.meaning: a market stand where goods are laid out for sale

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: to block progress, and a trader's booth showing wares.

clue.text: European country elected Democrat — smart guy getting back in

indicators.note: the turned name goes inside the other letters

parts.note: a party that is in has been elected

indicators.note: the name is turned round, read backwards

parts.note: a smart Alec is a know-it-all

explanation.surface: A European nation elects a Democrat, and a clever man returns to power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting back' reverses the smart guy's name, and 'in' signals the insertion. Smart Alec is a know-it-all.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Iceland is a Nordic island country in the North Atlantic.

clue.text: Contend river in swirling atmosphere is a holiday spot

indicators.note: the contend and river letters go inside
the air word is swirled, its letters rearranged

parts.note: air is the atmosphere around us
to vie is to compete or contend
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Competing currents in a turbulent sky over a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swirling' gives RIA, and 'in' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Riviera, on the French and Italian coast, is a famous resort area.

clue.text: Walk up

definitions.meaning: a long walk in the countryside
used as a verb, to raise, as with prices

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a long trek on foot, and to raise sharply, as a price rise.

clue.text: Unfeeling emperor's dismissing one in favour of son

indicators.note: the one, I, is removed and the son letters take its place

parts.note: imperial means belonging to an emperor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cold-hearted ruler sacks someone to make way for his son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismissing one in favour of' swaps the second I in IMPERIAL for SON.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: impersonal means lacking warmth or human feeling.
